newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi patches together parliamentary rift.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi patches together parliamentary rift.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi patched together his parliamentary majority on Thursday with a plea for unity after a rift with hard-left allies had threatened to pull his coalition apart.
But supporters and opposition alike questioned how long his centre-left government could keep the peace and maintain power.

Addressing the Senate (upper house) at the start of a debate on the future of his 11-month-old administration, Prodi said strong government was needed to complete wide-ranging reform and win Italy a place at the launch of the single European currency.
"This is not the time for uncertain, weak, transitionary governments," Prodi said. "This is the only government which can take the country into Europe."

Communist Refoundation, which secures Prodi's majority in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house), sent a shudder through the coalition on Wednesday by refusing to back the deployment of Italian troops in a security force for Albania.

The decision, taken for ideological reasons, forced the government to rely on support from centre-right parties to approve the operation and opened the way for confidence motions in both houses of parliament over the next three days.

With the Albanian mission ratified, Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said his party could once again rally behind Prodi. "Of course we will vote for the confidence motion," he told reporters after Prodi's speech.
But politicians from various parties doubted that Prodi could keep Refoundation in line for long.

"There's a problem. The cohesive, strong government that Prodi asks for, unhappily does not exist," said Cesare Salvi, parliamentary party leader of the coalition government's largest group, the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS).
He called for talks with Refoundation next week to make sure there was enough common ground to carry on working together.
Prodi spelt out ambitious plans for reform in his speech, saying a review of the Welfare State must be started immediately. "It cannot be put off a day longer," he said.
"It must...be clear that whoever gives us their confidence today must share the wide-ranging programme we have worked on and which we now want to bring to fruition," he added.
Prodi's coalition came to power last May but has always struggled to come to terms with the hardline Refoundation, which has blocked numerous government initiatives.

Bertinotti said earlier this week that the crunch would come over welfare reform. Many analysts believe that only cuts to the generous pensions system can guarantee heavily-indebted Italy a place in European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Refoundation is opposed to any reduction in social spending and Bertinotti said he was able to back Prodi in the confidence votes because he had left room for negotiations over the issue.
"In this area we will aim to bend the coalition towards the left. Not because we need this, but because the country needs it," Bertinotti said.
The confidence vote in the Senate is due around 1930 GMT, while the vote in the lower house is scheduled for Saturday.
